summary:
The Cook Islands are self-governing in free association with New Zealand. New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Cook Islanders, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male. Consent was explicitly not a defence. Reported maximum terms differ across sources: the 2017 coverage of the draft reform gives seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while later reporting on the repeal cites exposure of up to ten years for indecent acts between males. All sources agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the provisions from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited. The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 defines marriage as between a man and a woman, so a foreign same-sex marriage is not recognised locally and a trans visitor in a same-sex relationship has no spousal standing.

The repeal followed a protracted legislative path. A 2017 select committee recommended removing sections 154 and 155, and the provisions were struck from the draft Crimes Bill, which was drafted with New Zealand assistance; MPs subsequently backtracked. In October 2020 deferral continued when members again pushed the bill's report back, this time by three months, before the 2023 passage.
tangentialFactors:
The 1969 provisions were inherited through colonial-era legislation. Sources tracing the reform history describe the criminal taboo as introduced into a society that had been historically accepting of same-sex intimacy, which bears on how the local population and authorities regard the now-repealed offences.

The jurisdiction is small, with a population of roughly 21,000 recorded at the time of the 2017 reform effort. Visitors should expect limited institutional infrastructure: the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, has acted as the principal advocate before parliament.

The penalty figures cited for the former offences are inconsistent across reporting, ranging from five and seven years in the 2017 material to ten years in 2023 coverage. Nothing turns on the discrepancy now that the sections are repealed, but it reflects the thin documentation around a law that was never used.
localsOnly:
Te Tiare Association represented the Cook Islands LGBTI community in the reform process. Its submission was before the parliamentary select committee by August 2017, alongside submissions expected from at least three lawyers on penalties and sentencing, and a member of the association publicly described the 1969 provisions as homophobic.

The Crimes Amendment Bill that repealed sections 154 and 155 also strengthened protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault, so the 2023 reform package was not limited to consensual conduct.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources address sexual orientation offences and same-sex marriage. None provides sourced information on legal gender recognition, identity-document marker rules, or administrative procedures for changing gender on Cook Islands or New Zealand documents used locally; that layer of the record is unresolved.

No source identifies hate-crime legislation covering gender identity or expression, nor any provision restricting trans people from facilities, or any rule governing access to gender-affirming healthcare on the islands. Whether such rules exist under Cook Islands statute is unresolved rather than absent, and cannot be confirmed from the inventory.

The maximum penalty reported for the former sections 154 and 155 differs between sources (five, seven and ten years). The inventory does not resolve the correct statutory figures against the text of the 1969 Act.
